synthesis.headline: The transition Tlaloc tracked all week arrives: an amplified central-US trough with twin cold-core cutoffs replaces the old northern-Plains ridge, while the durable heat contracts south and west
synthesis.narrative:
The multi-day story reaches its turning point today. Where earlier this week a transient 594-dam ridge crowned the northern Plains, this morning's 500 mb analysis instead shows a strongly amplified longwave trough over the central Plains and upper Midwest, deep enough to close off two distinct cold-core circulations — one near 534 dam over Nebraska-Kansas, a second near 570 dam over the northern Rockies and Montana — with the coldest midlevel air co-located under both centers. This is the disruption Tlaloc has been anticipating since the northern anchor first let go five days ago: the ridge that had ruled the northern tier is gone, dug out and replaced by a slow, blocked trough. Flanking it, a western ridge over the Pacific Northwest and western Canada keeps dangerous heat over the West, and an eastern ridge near 588 dam holds over the Mid-Atlantic and New England, giving the CONUS a classic ridge-trough-ridge look. This is not a Rex block — there is no anticyclone stacked poleward of the cutoffs at the same longitude — but rather a quasi-stationary amplified trough with two cold cores, and the flow is slow to progress. Over Canada, a broad interior high (1025-1026 hPa over the western prairies, 1022-1023 hPa farther east) dominates the provinces, while a deep 994-hPa low sits over the Beaufort/high Arctic — the surface signature of the Arctic trough that the ensembles make the durable feature of the coming week.

Today's centers of action ring the trough and its jet corridor. The Air Mass RGB draws the boundary sharply: dry, subsident interior air arcs from the central Plains southeastward across the Tennessee Valley toward the Carolinas, its eastern edge against the moist green airmass marking the implied jet and baroclinic zone. SPC carries a Slight Risk across the northern Mid-Atlantic into the southern Northeast, where a weak disturbance crossing the Lower Great Lakes fires afternoon clusters in a moist airmass (~2000 J/kg MLCAPE) with damaging gusts of 50-65 mph before activity lines up toward the coast; a compact area of intense convection is already apparent over the Ohio Valley-to-Great Lakes region near the northeastern end of the boundary. A second, more uncertain threat runs along the surface trough and sagging front from the northern/central Plains into Minnesota, Iowa and Missouri, where upper-60s to 70s dewpoints support isolated large hail and severe gusts under weak large-scale forcing. High-based storms over eastern Colorado and terrain-driven storms over Arizona round out the day. The Day 2 outlook confirms this is a regime, not a one-off: northwesterly flow around the trough keeps a Slight Risk going Sunday from the northern Plains into the southern Great Lakes, with additional wind threats in Maine, the southern Appalachians and southeast Arizona. Meanwhile the western heat is the other headline — WPC flags 90s to over 110F, 7-12F above normal with potential records across the Desert Southwest and Intermountain West, driven by midlevel subsidence and warming under the western ridge, with wildfire smoke trapping poor air quality across the Pacific Northwest.

The upper pattern is what makes the near term coherent and the medium range decisive. The two cold-core cutoffs anchor the blocked flow and keep the central-US trough parked, so the frontal boundaries and northwest-flow convection it drives will linger rather than sweep through. The regime question — whether the ridge rebuilds behind this trough or genuinely retreats — is settled by the ensemble pair, and it settles the same way Tlaloc has been reading it. The 6-10 day (Aug 13-17) holds positive height anomalies of +4 to +6 dam over the central and eastern US but shows no western ridge amplification at all, with the zero line running down the Pacific coast and the dominant signal a deep Arctic trough (near -15 dam) over the Canadian Archipelago and Baffin. The 8-14 day (Aug 15-21) then pulls the ridge core still farther south, enclosing the southern Plains, Gulf Coast and Southeast within the 594-dam contour while western Canada, the northern Rockies and northern Plains sit near zero to weakly negative and the Arctic low deepens further. Comparing the two charts directly, the ridge is not regenerating in place — it is contracting toward the Southwest and southern tier while the north cools under a persistent, unusually deep high-latitude trough. This is transition-by-contraction, and today's dug-in central trough is the mechanism delivering it.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America running close to the seasonal script, with the North American Monsoon in full swing over the Southwest and northern Mexico and the WPC extended outlook expecting the ridge's southward retreat to keep moist southerly flow open across the southern tier next week. The ENSO backdrop is a developing warm state: the provided ONI table climbs from weak La Niña in late 2025 through neutral in late winter and into moderate El Niño by mid-2026, reaching roughly +0.95 to +1.39C for the spring-summer seasons, placing early August under a warm-ENSO influence — consistent with a subdued Atlantic against the climatological ramp toward the September hurricane peak. NHC keeps the Atlantic quiet (only a 20 percent tropical wave off Africa), while the eastern and central Pacific carry the activity: a central Pacific wave east-southeast of Hawaii at 60 percent, a wave southwest of Baja at 30 percent, and an area off southwestern Mexico at 20 percent over seven days. The daily teleconnection indices — a weakening, slightly negative PNA favoring eastern troughing over western ridging, a sharply positive AO reducing high-latitude blocking, and an NAO that has collapsed to strongly negative — are weak summer signals that lag the height field, but they cross-check the story the analysis and ensembles already tell: a western ridge losing its grip and a volatile, trough-dominated high-latitude circulation.
synthesis.regional_notes: One SPC mesoscale discussion is active (20 percent watch probability) over west-central Nebraska and southwestern South Dakota, where a subtle mid-level perturbation over the Badlands and Sandhills is destabilizing an airmass with CAPE over 2000 J/kg and strong deep-layer shear, supporting early-morning supercells with 1.5-2.5 inch hail, though upscale growth and a weakening nocturnal jet cloud its longevity past daybreak. Southwest monsoon moisture supports daily terrain thunderstorms with locally heavy rain and isolated flash flooding over Arizona and northwestern Mexico, with monsoon-trough convection also active near Baja and over the Yucatan. In the eastern Pacific, the Air Mass RGB flags a vigorous, organized convective cluster off the Pacific coast of Baja that warrants watching. Wildfire smoke continues to degrade air quality across the Pacific Northwest and Intermountain West under limited dispersion.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: The chart, valid 0900Z Saturday 08 August 2026, shows a sprawling high pressure complex dominating the central and eastern United States, with the most prominent center reading near 1021 mb over the lower Mississippi Valley/Tennessee region and additional cells labeled 1020 mb over the central Plains and the mid-Atlantic, none of which are strong enough on their own to be meteorologically noteworthy beyond reflecting a broadly anticyclonic surface pattern. A weak low near 1012 mb sits over the central High Plains with what appears to be a stationary or slowly moving frontal zone extending eastward across Kansas and Missouri into the Ohio Valley, with cold front symbols on its northern flank transitioning to warm front geometry further east — this boundary is the primary focus for surface convergence and moisture return across that corridor, where dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s F are plotted. Along the Pacific Northwest coast and into British Columbia, a modest low near 1010-1012 mb anchors a frontal system with a cold front pushing southward, backed surface winds visible in the plotted observations, though the gradient there is relatively tight compared to the slack isobar spacing across the interior West and the broad high over the Southeast. The tightest pressure gradient on the analysis appears to be along and just ahead of the central Plains frontal boundary, which combined with the moisture axis implied by the dewpoint readings in the mid-South and lower Missouri Valley, places the best surface-based lift focus from roughly eastern Kansas through Missouri and into the mid-South. Across the Desert Southwest, a diffuse surface trough is suggested by the loose pressure pattern and warm temperatures, consistent with typical monsoon-season surface heating, though no sharp boundaries are drawn there.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: The dominant feature over Canada proper is a sprawling high pressure regime across the interior, with centers labeled near 1025-1026 hPa evident over what appears to be the western prairies and a separate 1022-1023 hPa center over the central to eastern interior, producing a broadly anticyclonic pattern from roughly the Rockies eastward through Ontario and Quebec latitudes. A frontal boundary with warm and cold front segments is visible threading through the north-central portion of the continent, connecting a low near 994 hPa that sits well into the upper left of the frame, which given the polar projection places it over the high Arctic or Beaufort Sea region rather than over any province. Along the Canada-US border zone, the isobar spacing tightens noticeably across the central and eastern portions, suggesting a modest pressure gradient between the interior Canadian high and a cluster of low pressure and frontal activity over the north-central and northeastern United States, with lows in the 1008-1013 hPa range visible in what appears to be the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley area, implying a southerly fetch into the Great Lakes corridor and potentially focused lift along any residual frontal zone just north of the border. A separate area of frontal activity with a slow-moving or occluded system appears in the far upper-left corner of the frame, but its location is genuinely ambiguous under the polar projection and should not be placed closer than somewhere over the western Arctic or northeastern Pacific margins.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: The 500 mb pattern at 1200 UTC 8 August 2026 shows a strongly amplified longwave trough centered over the central Plains and upper Midwest, with closed height contours near 534 dam visible across the Nebraska-Kansas region and a second closed center apparent over the northern Rockies-Montana area near 570 dam, indicating two distinct cutoff or nearly cutoff circulations rather than a single open trough. The western closed low over the northern Rockies is separated from an amplified ridge axis over the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, while the eastern closed low over the central Plains sits beneath a region of tightly packed contours implying a strong implied jet corridor wrapping cyclonically around it; the tilt of the trough axis appears neutral to slightly negative (southwest to northeast) based on the contour geometry. The shading indicates 500 mb temperatures with the darkest brown cores co-located with the two closed lows, consistent with cold-core structure supporting the closed circulations. The eastern ridge visible from the Mid-Atlantic into New England shows heights near 588 dam, creating a broad ridge-trough-ridge pattern across the CONUS domain. Overall the flow appears blocked or at minimum very slow to progress, given the closed circulations and the strong amplitude separating the western ridge from the deep central trough; this configuration is more consistent with a quasi-stationary amplified trough with two cold-core centers than a classic Rex block, since no evident anticyclone sits meridionally poleward of the cutoff lows at the same longitude.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 1331Z 8 August 2026 shows a broad red-orange swath covering most of the continental interior from the Rockies eastward through the southern Plains and into the mid-South, consistent with dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under what is likely a broad summertime ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. A sharper, more elongated orange-to-green boundary arcs from the central Plains southeastward across the Tennessee Valley toward the Carolinas, marking the implied jet corridor and separating the drier continental air to the northwest from the moist green airmass to the southeast. Along and south of that boundary, scattered clusters of bright white deep convective tops are visible over the northern Gulf of Mexico, the western Caribbean, and Cuba, with an additional organized cluster off the Pacific coast of the Baja California Peninsula that appears vigorous and may warrant closer attention. A compact area of intense deep convection is also apparent over the Ohio Valley-to-Great Lakes region, embedded near the northeastern end of the airmass boundary. The northwestern corner of the domain transitions into purple-blue tones over the northern Rockies and Pacific Northwest, indicating cold, dry upper-level air on the poleward side of the flow, consistent with an upper trough or shortwave in that region.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: GOES-19 AirMass RGB, 08 August 2026 13:30Z. The dominant feature across the tropics and subtropics is an expansive green signature indicating deep, moist tropical air over Amazonia, the Caribbean, and much of the tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific, with scattered bright white convective tops concentrated over Central America, the southern Gulf of Mexico, and the Colombia-Venezuela border region. A sharp color transition from green to red-orange is visible along the western coast of South America and extending northwest across the subtropical eastern Pacific, consistent with dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under the South Pacific subtropical ridge. Two well-organized cyclonic systems with spiraling cloud structures are evident: one in the upper right of the frame over the central North Atlantic and another in the lower right over the South Atlantic near roughly 45-50 degrees south, both showing the tight banding characteristic of extratropical cyclones. Across southern South America, a broad orange-red airmass on the lee side of the Andes transitions abruptly to the cloudier and more disturbed Southern Ocean circulation, where the second cyclone is embedded in a curved cloud band consistent with an active extratropical wave. The high latitudes of northern Canada and the Arctic periphery display a mix of dark blue and muted tones suggesting cold, dry upper-tropospheric air, with no clearly organized jet-scale airmass boundary visible at the resolution of this full-disk frame.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most prominent warm signal covers the southern tier from the Desert Southwest through Texas and into the Southeast, where probabilities reach 80-90% above normal across much of the Gulf Coast region and climb to 90-100% over parts of southern Texas and coastal Louisiana, indicating a high-confidence heat signal. The Pacific Northwest and Alaska also carry above-normal probabilities in the 60-70% range, while Hawaii shows 50-60% above normal. In contrast, a coherent below-normal signal spans the Great Lakes and Northeast, with probabilities of 60-70% below normal centered on Michigan and the upper Ohio Valley, grading to leaning-below across the northern plains and into the mid-Atlantic. A broad near-normal zone separates the two regimes across the interior West and central plains, suggesting the boundary between the warm and cool air masses is positioned there with low forecast confidence in either direction. The sharp north-south dipole — above normal in the South and Southeast, below normal in the Great Lakes and Northeast — is geometrically consistent with a persistent amplified ridge over the South flanked by a trough or downstream shortwave influence over the eastern Great Lakes, implying that whatever pattern is driving current conditions is expected to continue rather than collapse within this period, though the near-normal swath across the Rockies and plains introduces some uncertainty about the ridge's exact position and amplitude.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, valid 13-17 August 2026. The dominant feature is a deep negative anomaly center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Baffin Island area, where the closed low in the height field sits near 546 dam with anomalies reading near -15 dam, making it the strongest negative center on the chart. A broad positive anomaly region covers much of the central and eastern contiguous United States, with values near +4 to +6 dam, consistent with a ridge axis that runs roughly from the central Plains northeastward toward the Great Lakes; the 588 dam contour bulges well into the southern and central US, and a 594 dam contour appears along the southeastern margin of the domain. The zero-anomaly line over western North America runs roughly along the Pacific Coast and into the interior Northwest, meaning little to no positive anomaly signal extends inland across the Rockies or the Great Basin, and the anomaly field there is near zero or slightly negative, indicating that any western ridge of recent weeks is not amplified in this period. The height pattern shows amplified meridional flow over Canada, with the trough axis implied by the deep Arctic low dropping southward over eastern Canada, but the contours across the contiguous US are becoming more zonal south of roughly 50°N, with tightly packed west-to-east running height lines across the northern tier. Overall, the pattern shows positive anomalies holding over the central and eastern US but no western ridge amplification, with the dominant anomaly signal being the cold Arctic trough rather than any high-latitude ridge over Alaska or western Canada.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a prognostic 500 mb heights and density (anomaly) product valid 15–21 August 2026, made 7 August 2026, with solid green contours for heights at 60 m intervals and dashed lines for anomalies. The dominant feature is a deep, closed low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, where heights fall to around 504–510 dam; the tightly packed contours imply a strong cyclonic circulation, and the anomaly dashes in that region are negative, consistent with a significant cold-core trough well above normal depth for August. Over the contiguous United States, heights ridge broadly across the southern tier, with the 594 dam contour enclosing an area from the southern Plains through the Gulf Coast and into the Southeast, placing the ridge core over the south-central and southeastern U.S. rather than over the northern Rockies or northern Plains; the anomaly contours in that region are positive, indicating an unseasonably amplified warm ridge. Western Canada and the northern Rockies through northern Plains fall in the transition zone between the Arctic low and the southern ridge, with heights around 552–576 dam and anomaly contours near zero to weakly negative, meaning no meaningful positive height anomaly is present over those regions — the ridge has retreated well to the south and west, closer to the Southwest and Gulf Coast, rather than being centered over the northern interior.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: A broad ridge of high pressure dominates the West through the weekend, driving dangerous heat across the Desert Southwest and Intermountain West with highs 90s to over 110F, 7-12F above normal and potential record temperatures. Heat spreads eastward early next week into the Central Plains and Mississippi Valley, reaching the Southeast by mid-week. Elevated fire danger and poor air quality from wildfire smoke will persist in the Pacific Northwest and Intermountain West due to limited smoke dispersion. Downstream, an upper-level trough drives frontal boundaries across the North-Central U.S., Northeast, and Mid-Atlantic, producing scattered showers and thunderstorms with enhanced activity along outflow boundaries. Isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms possible across the Northern Plains, Midwest, and Mid-Atlantic, capable of heavy rainfall. Southwest monsoon moisture supports daily thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding potential.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: SLIGHT RISK issued for northern Mid-Atlantic into southern Northeast, valid through early Sunday. Weak disturbance moving east across Lower Great Lakes will trigger scattered strong to severe thunderstorms this afternoon. Around 2000 J/kg MLCAPE with organized 700-250 mb flow supports damaging gusts (50-65 mph) and marginally severe hail before activity becomes more linear moving toward coast. Separately, strong instability across northern/central Plains into Minnesota/Iowa/Missouri with 60s-70s boundary layer dewpoints will support isolated to scattered storms developing near surface trough and sagging front, with large hail and severe gusts possible. High uncertainty due to weak forcing and model spread. Additional high-based convection possible eastern Colorado and western Kansas/Nebraska with isolated severe gusts. Arizona terrain storms expected evening with strong outflow gusts moving westward.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: West central Nebraska and southwestern South Dakota face potential for rapidly intensifying thunderstorms with large hail risk between 5-7 AM CDT. A subtle mid-level perturbation is enhancing ascent over the Badlands and Sandhills region. Increasing low-level moisture return and warm advection are destabilizing the atmosphere, with CAPE exceeding 2000 J/kg and strong deep-layer wind shear supporting supercell development. Storm initiation likely during 10-12Z timeframe. Uncertainty remains regarding threat duration post-daybreak due to upscale growth, continued warming aloft, and weakening nocturnal jet. Watch issuance probability 20 percent. Expected peak hail 1.5-2.5 inches.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
ATLANTIC: A tropical wave off West Africa's coast Tuesday has low near-term development potential but 20 percent chance of organization through seven days as it crosses the eastern and central tropical Atlantic.

EAST PACIFIC: Central Pacific tropical wave east-southeast of Hawaii shows medium potential with 60 percent seven-day formation chance; disorganized showers present with conducive conditions for gradual development early next week. Western East Pacific wave south-southwest of Baja California has low 30 percent seven-day chance; low pressure expected to form early next week with additional development possible. Offshore southwestern Mexico, potential low pressure area by mid-week with 20 percent seven-day development chance.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ONI values show a transition from weak La Niña conditions in late 2025 through early 2026 (anomalies around -0.6 to -0.2°C) toward warming through spring 2026. By February-March 2026, anomalies turn slightly positive. The trend accelerates into late spring, with anomalies reaching +0.95 to +1.39°C by April-July 2026, indicating a shift toward El Niño development. Sea surface temperatures are steadily warming across all three-month periods shown.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA has weakened to -0.70 (7-day mean), drifting negative; currently favors eastern troughing over western ridging. AO has strengthened sharply to +0.37, reversing from -0.05 a week prior; supports lower Arctic heights and reduced high-latitude blocking. NAO has collapsed to -0.90, falling from +0.19 last week; today at -1.28, lowest in the sequence. Negative NAO favors Atlantic blocking and may trap eastern upper-level troughs. Note: summer teleconnections are inherently weak; these indices provide directional context only.
